Lessons.Title: Being Skeptical
ExplanationParagraphs: Source-aligned goals: Critique and evaluate reports (orally) based on data and how the data were collected. Recognize the purposes of and differences among sample surveys, experiments, and observational studies. Understand statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters based on data from a statistical study.

A statistical conclusion depends on how data were collected. A sample survey estimates a population; a randomized experiment can support causal inference; an observational study may show association but cannot automatically establish causation. Voluntary responses can be biased.

Source activity 1.1: Notice and Wonder: Headlines: A graph and 2 headlines from a website are shown. What do you notice? KeyConcepts.Title: Assess statistical claims critically
KeyConcepts.Definition: A statistical conclusion depends on how data were collected. A sample survey estimates a population; a randomized experiment can support causal inference; an observational study may show association but cannot automatically establish causation. Voluntary responses can be biased.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Apply the exact task conditions, mathematical operation, and permitted domain.
KeyConcepts.Example: A web poll of 100 volunteers reports 90% support for a policy. Does that prove 90% of the whole city supports it? Answer: No; the citywide percentage is not established.

KeyConcepts.Title: Source-context verification
KeyConcepts.Definition: A model must be checked against the given quantities and representation.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep source index, signs, units, factor structure and forbidden inputs.
KeyConcepts.Example: Voluntary response is not a probability sample; participants may differ systematically from nonparticipants.

KeyConcepts.Title: Apply the learning goal to independent practice
KeyConcepts.Definition: Understand statistics as a process for making inferences about population parameters based on data from a statistical study.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For a new set of inputs, use the lesson's model, show the intermediate steps and check the allowed domain, units and interpretation.
KeyConcepts.Example: A school surveys only students attending an optional club about all students' habits. Identify the risk. Answer: Selection bias: club members are not a random school sample.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying an algebraic solution at an excluded input.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A zero denominator or impossible physical quantity makes the result invalid.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State and check the domain before finalising.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Guessing a graph shape without source-specific reasoning.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Multiplicity, degree, leading sign and context can alter the curve.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Explain each relevant feature using algebra, a table or verified source activity.
